title: Heracles
wiki_lead:
Heracles (   Ancient Greek: Ἡρακλῆς, lit. 'glory/fame of Hera'), born Alcaeus (Ἀλκαῖος) or Alcides (Ἀλκείδης), was the greatest of the Greek heroes. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and the foster son of Amphitryon. He was thought to be both a hero and a god, possessing superhuman strength. No tomb was ever identified as his, and at some festivals sacrifice was offered to him first as a hero and then as a god. He was widely worshipped as a patron of young men and gymnasia.
Heracles appears in numerous myths, which often involve the enmity of Hera, the wife of Zeus. Driven mad by Hera, Heracles killed his wife Megara and their children. Heracles performed a series of labours, conventionally numbered twelve, on the orders of his cousin Eurystheus, the king of Argos. These tasks included the killing of the Nemean lion and the Lernaean Hydra, the theft of the golden apples of the Hesperides, and the capture of Cerberus. Episodes outside the cycle of labours have him sailing with the Argonauts, sacking Troy in the generation before the Trojan War, freeing Prometheus, and serving a further term of slavery to Omphale, queen of Lydia. 
Heracles married multiple times and fathered a large number of children; his descendants are called the Heracleidae. Ancient tradition also records several male lovers, including Iolaus and Hylas. According to the story of Heracles's apotheosis, his wife Deianira (who had been deceived by the dying centaur Nessus) gave him a garment smeared with poisoned blood. Unable to remove it, he immolated himself atop Mount Oeta, burning away his mortal part. He ascended to Olympus as a god, and married the goddess Hebe.
His Roman form is called Hercules; Roman emperors, such as Commodus and Maximian, often identified themselves with him. Heracles remains a frequent subject of Western art and popular culture.

Origin
Many popular stories were told of his life, the most famous being the twelve Labours of Hercules; Alexandrian poets of the Hellenistic age drew his mythology into a high poetic and tragic atmosphere. His figure, which initially drew on Near Eastern motifs such as the lion-fight, was widely known.
Heracles was the greatest of Hellenic chthonic heroes, but unlike other Greek heroes, no tomb was identified as his. Heracles was both hero and god, as Pindar says heros theos; at the same festival sacrifice was made to him, first as a hero, with a chthonic libation, and then as a god, upon an altar: thus he embodies the closest Greek approach to a "demi-god".
The core of the story of Heracles has been identified by Walter Burkert as originating in Neolithic hunter culture and traditions of shamanistic crossings into the netherworld. It is possible that the myths surrounding Heracles were based on the life of a real person or several people whose accomplishments became exaggerated with time.


Hero or god
Heracles's role as a culture hero, whose death could be a subject of mythic telling (see below), was accepted into the Olympian Pantheon during Classical times. This created an awkwardness in the encounter with Odysseus in the episode of Odyssey XI, called the Nekuia, where Odysseus encounters Heracles in Hades:

Ancient critics were aware of the problem of the aside that interrupts the vivid and complete description, in which Heracles recognizes Odysseus and hails him, and some modern critics deny that the verse's beginning, in Fagles's translation His ghost I mean ..., was part of the original composition: "once people knew of Heracles's admission to Olympus, they would not tolerate his presence in the underworld", remarks Friedrich Solmsen, noting that the interpolated verses represent a compromise between conflicting representations of Heracles.

grok_lead: Heracles (Greek: á¼©ÏÎ±ÎºÎ»á¿Ï, HÄraklÄs), known to the Romans as Hercules, was a legendary divine hero in ancient Greek mythology, renowned for his superhuman strength, courage, and the completion of twelve monumental labors that established him as the greatest of all Greek heroes. Born to Zeus, the king of the Olympian gods, and the mortal woman Alcmene, daughter of Electryon, Heracles' conception resulted from Zeus disguising himself as Alcmene's husband Amphitryon and extending the night threefold to ensure his birth. From infancy, he faced the wrath of Hera, Zeus 's jealous wife, who sent two serpents to kill him in his cradle; Heracles strangled them with his bare hands, demonstrating his prodigious might even as a baby. As a young man, Heracles accidentally killed his music teacher Linus in a fit of anger and later, driven mad by Hera, slew his wife Megara and their children, prompting him to seek purification at the oracle of Delphi. The oracle commanded him to serve King Eurystheus of Mycenae for twelve years, during which he performed the famous Twelve Labors: slaying the invulnerable Nemean Lion, destroying the multi-headed Lernaean Hydra, capturing the Golden Hind of Artemis, capturing the Erymanthian Boar, cleaning the Augean stables, slaying the Stymphalian Birds, capturing the Cretan Bull, stealing the man-eating Mares of Diomedes, obtaining the girdle of Hippolyta, fetching the cattle of the monster Geryon, stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides, and finally capturing the three-headed guard dog Cerberus from the Underworld. These feats, accomplished over eight years and a month, not only atoned for his crimes but also rid the world of numerous monsters and established Heracles as a protector of humanity and a culture hero who brought civilization through his exploits. Beyond the labors, Heracles participated in heroic quests such as joining the Argonauts on their voyage for the Golden Fleece, aiding the gods in the Gigantomachy against the Giants, and liberating Prometheus from his eternal torment. In his later life, he married Deianira, but tragically died after being poisoned by a tunic soaked in the blood of the centaur Nessus, whom he had slain; his mortal part burned away on a funeral pyre atop Mount Oeta, allowing his divine essence to ascend to Olympus, where he was reconciled with Hera, married her daughter Hebe, and achieved full godhood. Worshipped across the ancient world in temples, shrines, and festivals from Greece to Asia Minor, North Africa, and Spain, Heracles symbolized strength, perseverance, and the triumph of order over chaos, influencing art, literature, and philosophy for millennia.
